name: undo
tagline: Undo what the last shell command did to the filesystem
description: undo is the safety net the shell never had: it reverts exactly what the last command did to your filesystem, on any filesystem, without root. There is no snapshotting and no daemon — a shell hook arms a small LD_PRELOAD library around every command, which journals destructive libc calls and saves affected files into a per-command session before they happen. Deletions are preserved by hardlink, so rm -rf on gigabytes copies no data, and replaying the journal in reverse relinks deleted files, moves renames back, and swaps truncated files with their backups. It catches the classic mistakes: rm -rf, mv over a file you needed, > truncation, accidental chmod -R, and script-created files. undo redo re-applies a reverted session, a session store keeps the last 30 commands within a 1 GiB budget, and everything is plain files you can inspect. It works for zsh, bash, and fish, and supports undo run for arming a single command without a hook.
highlights: Reverts exactly what one command touched — command-granular, not time-granular
LD_PRELOAD shim journals destructive syscalls, no daemon and no setup habits
Hardlink backups make rm -rf on gigabytes instant and nearly free
undo redo re-applies, with interactive cherry-picking and diff inspection
Works three processes deep inside build tools where aliases cannot reach
curatorNote: The undo the shell never had: it journals destructive syscalls and hardlinks backups so you can undo rm -rf, mv clobbers, and > truncation. 366 stars in two weeks says the pain was real — this is the kind of tool you install once and forget until the day it saves you.
